entry: Polish footballer and captain of the Poland national team. He plays as a striker and is one of only five players to have scored 100 goals with three different clubs. He ranks third among all-time goalscorers in the [[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]], with 109 goals, and won the Best FIFA Men's Player Award in 2020 and 2021. He also won the European Golden Shoe for the 2020–21 and 2021–22 seasons. In June 2026 he joined Major League Soccer club Chicago Fire.

Scottish novelist, essayist, poet and travel writer. Born and educated in [[Edinburgh]], he suffered from serious bronchial trouble for much of his life but wrote prolifically and traveled widely. He is best known for the novels *Treasure Island* (1883), *Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde* (1886) and *Kidnapped* (1886), and for the poetry collection *A Child's Garden of Verses* (1885). As a young man he received encouragement from London literary circles, and W. E. Henley may have provided the model for Long John Silver in *Treasure Island*. He later settled in [[Samoa]], where his writing turned from romance and adventure fiction toward a darker realism. A celebrity in his lifetime, his critical reputation has fluctuated since his death, although his works are now held in general acclaim. In 2018 he was ranked just behind [[Charles Dickens]] as the 26th-most-translated author in the world.

American experimental physicist. Millikan won the 1923 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the [[Elementary charge|elementary charge]] of electricity and on the [[Photoelectric effect|photoelectric effect]]. His oil-drop experiment measured the charge of the [[Electron|electron]], and he verified Einstein's photoelectric equation experimentally. He earned a Doctor of Philosophy from [[Columbia University]] in 1895 and joined the [[University of Chicago]] in 1896, becoming professor of physics in 1910. From 1921 to 1945 he chaired the Executive Council of the California Institute of Technology, helping to turn it into one of the leading research institutions in the United States. He also conducted research on [[Cosmic ray|cosmic rays]], served as vice-chairman of the National Research Council during [[World War I]], and coauthored a popular and influential series of introductory physics textbooks.

American actor and singer known for antihero roles and film noir. He received an Academy Award nomination for Best Supporting Actor for *The Story of G.I. Joe* (1945), and his best-known films include *Out of the Past* (1947) and *The Night of the Hunter* (1955). He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1984 and the Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award in 1992. [[Roger Ebert]] called him his favorite movie star and the soul of film noir.

Zimbabwean revolutionary and politician; first prime minister (1980–1987) and second president (1987–2017) of [[Zimbabwe]]. He was imprisoned from 1964 to 1974, after which he directed guerrilla operations from exile in Mozambique as leader of the Zimbabwe African National Union. He oversaw ZANU's role in the [[Rhodesian Bush War]], and after the 1980 independence election he expanded healthcare and education. His 5th Brigade crushed opposition in Matabeleland during the Gukurahundi campaign (1982–1987), which killed at least 20,000 people. From 2000 he encouraged seizures of white-owned farms, and food production collapsed amid famine and hyperinflation. He was re-elected in 2002, 2008 and 2013, and critics accused his campaigns of violence and electoral fraud. Supporters praised him as a hero who helped free Zimbabwe from British colonialism; critics accused him of dictatorship, economic mismanagement, corruption and human rights abuses. In 2017 members of his party ousted him in a coup.

English actor and producer known for both studio films and independent productions. He achieved global fame as Edward Cullen in *The Twilight Saga*, whose five films grossed over $3.3 billion worldwide. He later worked with auteur directors, including [[David Cronenberg]] on *Cosmopolis* (2012), and starred in [[Christopher Nolan]]'s *Tenet* (2020) and *The Batman* (2022). [[Time (magazine)|Time]] ranked him among the 100 most influential people in the world. He founded the production company Icki Eneo Arlo and has been the face of Dior Homme fragrance since 2013.

British Conservative statesman and prime minister of the United Kingdom (1834–1835, 1841–1846). As Home Secretary he reformed the criminal law and created the modern police force, whose officers became known as "bobbies" and "peelers" in tribute to him. Peel was one of the founders of the modern [[Conservative Party (UK)|Conservative Party]], and his Tamworth Manifesto of December 1834 laid down its principles. He reversed his stance on Catholic emancipation and supported the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829. As prime minister he cut tariffs, replaced the lost revenue with a 3 percent [[Income tax|income tax]], and set up a modern banking system. His decision to join with Whigs and Radicals to repeal the Corn Laws in 1846 led to his resignation. Historian [[A. J. P. Taylor]] wrote that Peel was "in the first rank of 19th-century statesmen."

English singer and songwriter, lead singer of [[Led Zeppelin]] from its founding in 1968 until the band broke up in 1980. He later pursued a successful solo career and collaborated with bluegrass artist Alison Krauss; their album *Raising Sand* won the Grammy Award for Album of the Year in 2009. Regarded by many as one of the greatest singers in [[Rock music|rock music]], he is known for his powerful, wide-ranging voice. [[Rolling Stone]] ranked him one of the 100 best singers of all time in 2008.

American actor, director and producer, celebrated as a leading man of the American New Wave. He achieved stardom in *Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid* (1969) and *The Sting* (1973), which earned him an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] nomination for Best Actor. *Ordinary People* (1980), his directing debut, won four Academy Awards, including Best Picture and Best Director. He co-founded the Sundance Institute and Sundance Film Festival to support independent filmmakers, and he was noted for environmental activism and support for Indigenous rights.

German composer, pianist and critic of the early Romantic era. His works typify the spirit of the Romantic era in German music. Schumann studied law at [[Leipzig]] before turning to music, and in 1834 he co-founded the *Neue Zeitschrift für Musik*, which he edited for ten years. His early piano pieces include *Carnaval* and *Kinderszenen* (1834–1838), and his song cycles include *Dichterliebe*. He married pianist Clara Wieck in 1840 despite her father's bitter opposition. From 1850 he was music director in [[Düsseldorf]], but he had to resign after three years. In 1853 he met the young [[Johannes Brahms]], whom he praised in print. His mental health declined, and in 1854 he threw himself into the [[Rhine]] before spending his last years in a sanatorium near [[Bonn]]. Composers inspired by his music include [[Gustav Mahler]], [[Claude Debussy]] and [[Maurice Ravel]].

English actor and writer. He began in theatre with the Shakespeare Memorial Theatre and the Old Vic, mostly in Shakespearean roles, and he was nominated for an Academy Award and a Golden Globe for playing [[Henry VIII]] in *A Man for All Seasons* (1966). His film roles included the shark hunter Quint in *Jaws* (1975) and the mobster Doyle Lonnegan in *The Sting* (1973). He won the 1962 Hawthornden Prize for his novel *The Sun Doctor*. His novel and play *The Man in the Glass Booth* earned a Tony Award nomination for Best Play.

American man, the tallest person in recorded history for whom there is irrefutable evidence. Born in Alton, Illinois, near [[St. Louis]], he reached a height of 8 ft 11.1 in (2.72 m). His great size resulted from hypertrophy of the [[Pituitary gland|pituitary gland]], which produced abnormally high levels of human growth hormone. He toured with the Ringling Brothers Circus in 1936, appearing in everyday clothes rather than as a sideshow act. A faulty brace irritated his ankle and led to [[Infection|infection]], which was treated with a [[Blood transfusion|blood transfusion]] and surgery.

American actor known for the television series *It Takes a Thief*, *Switch* and *Hart to Hart*. He had recurring roles on *Two and a Half Men* and *NCIS*, and his films included *Prince Valiant* (1954), *The Towering Inferno* (1974) and the *Austin Powers* trilogy, in which he played Number 2. In 2018 the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department named Wagner a "person of interest" in the investigation into the death of his first wife, actress [[Natalie Wood]]. Wagner has denied any involvement.

British Whig statesman, regarded as the de facto first prime minister of Great Britain (1721–1742). Born in [[Norfolk]] into the local gentry and educated at [[Eton College]], he was elected to Parliament in 1701. He held the posts of First Lord of the Treasury, chancellor of the Exchequer and leader of the House of Commons, and he remains the longest-serving prime minister in UK history, with a tenure of over 20 years. His appointment as chancellor of the Exchequer after the South Sea Bubble stock-market crisis of 1720 drew attention to perceived protection of political allies. He worked for peace, lower taxes and growing exports, and allowed a little more tolerance for Protestant Dissenters. His dominance was dubbed the "Robinocracy." Historian H. T. Dickinson credited him with safeguarding the Hanoverian succession and defending the principles of the [[Glorious Revolution]].

American filmmaker known for blending cutting-edge visual effects with storytelling. He directed the *Back to the Future* trilogy (1985–1990) and *Who Framed Roger Rabbit* (1988), and he won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Director for *Forrest Gump* (1994). He explored motion-capture techniques in animated films such as *The Polar Express* (2004), *Beowulf* (2007) and *A Christmas Carol* (2009). He has collaborated with composer Alan Silvestri since 1984, and he has directed [[Tom Hanks]] in five films.

King of Scots from 1306 to 1329, popularly known as Robert the Bruce. He led Scotland during the First War of Scottish Independence and is regarded in Scotland as a national hero. As Earl of Carrick he took part in [[William Wallace]]'s campaign against [[Edward I]] of England. After being crowned in March 1306, he was defeated at Methven and forced into hiding, but he re-emerged in 1307 to wage a highly successful guerrilla war. At the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314 he defeated a much larger English army under [[Edward II]]. In 1320 Scottish nobles submitted the Declaration of Arbroath to the [[Pope|pope]], asserting Scotland's status as an independent kingdom, and in 1324 the pope recognized him as king. The 1328 Treaty of Edinburgh–Northampton saw [[Edward III]] renounce all claims to sovereignty over Scotland.

Legendary heroic outlaw of English folklore, later featured in literature, theater and film. He is traditionally depicted as a highly skilled [[Archery|archer]] and swordsman dressed in Lincoln green, and he is most closely associated with the practice of "robbing the rich to give to the poor." In the oldest versions he is a member of the yeoman class, while some modern retellings make him a noble who fought in the [[Crusades|Crusades]]. His band of outlaws, the Merry Men, includes his lover, Maid Marian, and his chief opponent is the Sheriff of Nottingham. The earliest known [[Ballad|ballads]] about him date from the 15th century, and they stress his partisanship of the common people and his [[Anti-clericalism|anti-clericalism]]. Historians and folklorists have proposed at least eight plausible origins for the legend, and some suggest "Robin Hood" was a stock alias for bandits.

American actor and comedian known for improvisational skills and a wide range of characters. He rose to fame as the alien Mork in the sitcom *Mork & Mindy* and received his first leading film role in *Popeye* (1980). He won an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Supporting Actor for *Good Will Hunting* (1997), and his other Oscar-nominated roles included *Good Morning, Vietnam* and *Dead Poets Society*. He also starred in *Mrs. Doubtfire* (1993) and provided voice work in *Aladdin* (1992). He is regarded as one of the greatest comedians of all time.

English adventure novel by [[Daniel Defoe]], first published in 1719. It is often credited as marking the beginning of realistic fiction in the English language, and it combines epistolary, confessional and didactic forms. The title character is cast away and spends 28 years on a remote tropical island near the coasts of [[Venezuela]] and Trinidad before being rescued. The story is thought to be based on the life of Alexander Selkirk, a Scottish castaway who lived for four years on a Pacific island now part of [[Chile]]. The first edition credited Crusoe as its author, and many readers believed he was a real person. Before the end of 1719 the book had run through four editions, and it has inspired so many imitations that its name defines a genre, the Robinsonade.

Online game platform and game creation system developed by Roblox Corporation. Users create games with Roblox Studio using Luau, a modified dialect of [[Lua]], and developers can exchange earned Robux for real-world currency through the Developer Exchange program. As of February 2025 the platform reported an average of 85.3 million daily active users. It has faced criticism over child safety and content moderation, and it has been restricted or blocked in [[China]], [[Egypt]], [[Turkey]] and [[Iraq]].

1987 American science fiction action film directed by Paul Verhoeven. Set in a crime-ridden near-future [[Detroit]], *RoboCop* follows police officer Alex Murphy, who is murdered by criminals and rebuilt by the corporation Omni Consumer Products as the cyborg law enforcer RoboCop. Filmed mainly in [[Dallas]], Texas, it grossed $53.4 million on its release. Its themes include corporate greed, and it is seen as a rebuke of the era's Reaganomics policies. It spawned sequels, including *RoboCop 2* (1990) and *RoboCop 3* (1993), and a remake was released in 2014.

Interdisciplinary study and practice of the design, construction, operation and use of [[Robot|robots]]. Robotics usually combines four aspects of design work: a power source, mechanical construction, a control system, and software run by [[Remote control|remote control]] or [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]]. The goal of most robotics is to design machines that assist humans in fields such as agriculture, construction, medicine, the military, mining, [[Space exploration|space exploration]] and transportation. Robots can displace workers, and some expect this to accelerate, leading to proposals such as basic income. The first industrially deployed robot arm, the Unimate, was installed at a General Motors plant in 1961. Electric motors are the most popular actuators, and robots may be powered by batteries, [[Solar power|solar power]] or, in space, [[Nuclear power|nuclear power]].

Distance from a celestial body within which a second body, held together only by its own gravity, disintegrates. Named after the French astronomer Édouard Roche, who first calculated it in 1848, the limit depends on the radius of the second body and the ratio of the two bodies' [[Density|densities]]. Inside it, orbiting material disperses and forms [[Ring system|rings]], while outside it material tends to coalesce. Almost all known planetary rings lie within their Roche limits, and a weak [[Comet|comet]] can break apart when it passes inside one.

City in western [[New York (state)|New York]] (pop., 2020: 211,328), county seat of Monroe County. It is New York's fourth-most populous city, and the surrounding metropolitan area has an estimated 1.05 million residents. Rochester grew rapidly as a flour-milling center on the Genesee River and later became a manufacturing hub for companies including Eastman Kodak, Xerox and Bausch & Lomb. The city was also a hub for [[Abolitionism|abolitionism]] and the women's rights movement. Its population declined with deindustrialization in the late 20th century, though less severely than other [[Rust Belt|Rust Belt]] cities.

American actor, one of the most popular film stars of Hollywood's Golden Age. He achieved stardom in *Magnificent Obsession* (1954), *All That Heaven Allows* (1955) and *Giant* (1956), for which he received an Academy Award nomination for Best Actor. He also starred in romantic comedies with [[Doris Day]], including *Pillow Talk* (1959). Hudson later turned to television, starring in *McMillan & Wife* (1971–1977). He was discreet about his sexual orientation. In 1985 he publicly disclosed his AIDS diagnosis, and he was the first major American celebrity to die from an AIDS-related illness.
